articles.title: Calavera Cabina: a tribute app for Día de Muertos
articles.description: The booth that didn't happen Picture this: it's spooky season, late October, and you are building a booth for a conference. People are getting creative: on the left, someone has a tarot card activity with a crystal ball and are saging your codebases against bugs. On the right, folks are handing out Halloween candy with the phrase, "You're worth a mint to us". I wanted to build a seasonal experience that would lean into Cloudinary's new image generation tooling: people walk up, take a selfie, and leave with a generated sticker. The catch: I only have a thermal printer on hand, but what about creating something in black and white, like a tatoo? What about printing a stylized selfie that reflects an interesting seasonal image? What about Día de Muertos? Mexico's famous holiday full of rich symbolism and imagery such as colorful, fashionable skeletons, cut paper garlands, brilliant florals, and more. Because of some logistic snafus, the seasonal booth experience for conference didn't materialize. The app is built, however, so I wanted to share it, taking you along with me down the rabbit hole into scary stories and legends. A colorful prototype Why Día de Muertos If you're on "spookytok" - TikTok's Halloween stream, you'll soon hear a beautiful song, "La Llorona" - the weeping woman. Depending on the interpretation, she is a woman who cries for her lost children or her lost love, wandering by waterways (something like the Irish Banshee), wailing. Often the song is paired with images of the "Calavera Catrina", a stylish skeleton lady (more below). Could we create a transformation of a selfie into La Llorona? An authentic image of the Wailing Lady is more like a tragic figure than a saucy skeleton: Me as La Llorona, not a cheerful image I hesitated. Is it too sad an image? We want people to view themselves as taking part in a festive event, not a funeral! And moreover, for the men coming to the booth, how would we visualize them? Is there a wailing banshee equivalent? This took me down quite a journey away from Mexico and into Venezuela, where we encounter El Silbón, "The Whistler", a lost soul carrying a bag on his back, whistling a warning of imminent doom to passersby. It's a really scary story, far too much for the unwary folks who would wander to our booth! My long-suffering husband as El Silbon It was time to return to the brighter aesthetic of Día de Muertos. The imagery that works best is the true Catrina or Catrin - the familiar fashionable skeleton celebrated with face painting and costumes. Catrina was popularized in the early 1900s by Mexican artist Jose Guadalupe Posada: La Calavera Catrina, c. 1910, lithograph She and her dandy skeleton counterpart, El Catrín, poke sly fun at the Europeanized gentry of the time, while also drawing on a the much older traditions of the Aztec queen of the underworld, Mictēcacihuātl, mixed with Catholic imagery around All Saint's Day. source On TikTok, we have ladies dressed in their finest Catrina garb paired with the haunting Llorona song...an interestingly mixed metaphor. It took me a little while to get the aesthetic where I wanted it: spooky, but not scary. Now, for the prompt! With AI, it's trivially easy to scaffold an app that will take your selfie and use Cloudinary's Image Generation tooling to generate something that would work for my little thermal printer. The trick is to get the prompt right. I experimented several times to find something that would print well, produce a recognizable portrait, and be true to the aesthetic of the Catrina: "Restyle the person in [1] as a Día de Muertos-inspired fine-line tattoo portrait. " + "Preserve their identity, facial features, hairstyle, proportions, and recognizable expression. " + "Use crisp black ink on a pure white background with delicate tattoo-flash linework, " + "clean contours, restrained stippling, strong negative space, and clear details that print well at small size. " + "Use dignified ceremonial clothing inspired by traditional Mexican portraiture: an elegant embroidered blouse, " + "dress, rebozo, lace-trimmed neckline, or formal charro-inspired garment. " + "Avoid modern casual clothing, business attire, exposed cleavage, costume-like clothing, or generic fantasy garments. " + "Keep the face human and recognizable rather than replacing it with a skull. " + "No color, grayscale, gradients, painterly shading, beige texture, photorealism, text, or watermark."; Then, in this very simple Astro app, send that prompt along with the image to the Image Generation API: body: JSON.stringify({ prompt: stylePrompts[style as keyof typeof stylePrompts], reference_images: [{ source_type: 'managed_asset', asset_id: upload.asset_id }], model: { mode: 'auto', preference: 'quality' }, image_size: { aspect_ratio: '3:4', resolution: '1K' }, target: { target_type: 'managed_asset', public_id: `calavera-cabina/portraits/${crypto.randomUUID()}`, }, }), The use of 'mode: 'auto'' allows the choice of a model that will work best for your prompt. Depending on your model, you might get a different result, so it's important to have a good prompt (AI can help with crafting one): One model kept building interesting frames and using spiderweb images for some reason, so I had to rework the prompt How Calavera Cabina works I can't take credit for the clever pun (thanks, Lovable!) - but the Calavera Cabina (Skeleton Camera, as opposed to the Calavera Catrina), was starting to take shape. Home screen of the Cabina I decided to give users a choice. Let them take a selfie and choose a style, leaning on imagery of the Catrin/Catrina, or a floral motif style, or a darker, mystical night style reflecting the Llorona mood. They all turned out beautifully! The final result An invitation I want to be extremely respectful of cultural norms and local holidays, and I know I'm approaching this as an outsider. From a self-education standpoint, I was really happy that my meanderings with this app concept led me into new sources of knowledge. It's fascinating to me to find parallels between the stories of Celtic water-wanderers I grew up with and the crying lady of Mexico. But the Día de Muerto's particular aesthetic seems to stand out as a delightfully spooky, deliciously fun celebration of deep culture. I invite you to check out the codebase and fork it to try the app yourself. You'll need an API Key and Secret alongside your Cloud Name, an upload preset for your images, and the Image Generation Add-On: https://github.com/cloudinary-devs/photo-booth. Print yourself a tatoo-style sticker! And Happy Halloween, Día de Muertos, and All Saint's Day! The printed sticker result Cloudinary ❤️ developers Ready to level up your media workflow? Start using Cloudinary for free and build better visual experiences today. 👉 Create your free account Shout-out to the folks I consulted with on this article: Diego from Colombia 🇨🇴 and Anthar from Mexico 🇲🇽 💕

articles.title: The Last Light: Keeping Memories Alive with Local, Open-Weight AI 🕯️
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge — Week 4: Ghost in the Machine. What I Built What if the most meaningful use of AI wasn't answering questions, writing code, or automating work—but helping us keep the stories we never want to forget? That question inspired The Last Light, a cinematic, privacy-first AI memory keeper built around the idea that memories deserve a place to live, without having to leave the devices where they are stored. The Last Light brings together the atmosphere of a candlelit remembrance altar, the intimacy of a personal journal, and the creative possibilities of open-weight AI. Here is what it offers: The Digital Ofrenda: An interactive remembrance altar featuring candlelight, marigolds, photographs, and personal dedications. The Memory Archive: A personal space for preserving names, dates, family stories, favorite foods, songs, meaningful places, and photographs. Let the Memory Speak: A local AI writing studio that transforms a memory into a first-person remembrance, a heartfelt letter, an atmospheric story, a poem, or a family chronicle. Private by design: Memories and photographs are stored locally in the browser, with tools for exporting and restoring personal archives. Offline-oriented AI: Open-weight language models can run directly in the browser on compatible hardware, rather than requiring every generation request to go through a hosted AI service. The goal isn't to make a machine pretend it can bring someone back. It's to give people a thoughtful way to preserve the details, stories, and little things that make a memory meaningful. Demo 🕯️ Experience The Last Light: https://the-last-light.ai.studio/ Explore the experience, discover the digital ofrenda, and try the memory-writing studio on a compatible device. The first model download requires an internet connection. Local generation depends on browser support, available device resources, and the model being downloaded successfully. Code 💻 GitHub repository: https://github.com/babuyasinghchauhan-eng/the_last_light The project is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, and WebLLM, with browser-native storage and a design focused on privacy and data portability. The repository includes the source code, project documentation, and an MIT license for the application. The model weights have their own respective licenses. Contributions, improvements, and ideas are welcome. How I Built It I approached this as a local-first application rather than a conventional chatbot wrapped in a beautiful interface. The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS. The visual direction combines cinematic lighting, dark editorial layouts, candlelight, and marigold-inspired details to create an experience that feels more like entering a quiet digital sanctuary than opening another AI dashboard. For the AI layer, I used WebLLM, which enables language-model inference in the browser using supported WebGPU execution paths. The application is designed to work with quantized open-weight models, including options from the Qwen2.5 and SmolLM2 families. Model selection and actual inference depend on the model configuration and the device's capabilities. Instead of sending personal memories to a remote LLM endpoint, the writing studio passes the user's chosen memory and writing instructions to the locally running model. The model then generates a literary interpretation of those details. The prompts are designed to preserve the user's supplied information, avoid inventing biographical facts as truth, and treat first-person writing as a creative device rather than a claim of communication with a deceased person. For persistence, the application uses IndexedDB to keep memories and photographs in the browser. Export and restore functionality gives users a way to retain control over their own collection. A few technical realities are worth acknowledging: The initial application and model downloads require connectivity. Subsequent offline use depends on assets and model files being cached and available, along with a compatible browser and sufficient device resources. Local inference is not equally fast on every device, and WebGPU support can vary. Open-weight models have their own license terms, which must be respected independently of the application's MIT license. These constraints are part of the engineering challenge. Running AI locally is not magic; it is a trade-off between control, privacy, hardware requirements, and convenience. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Because a memory is too personal to treat as just another API request. Many AI experiences depend on sending prompts and data to a service controlled by someone else. That can be useful, but it also introduces external dependencies, usage limits, potential costs, and questions about where personal information goes. The Last Light explores another approach. 1. Privacy should be an architectural decision. Family photographs, personal stories, and intimate memories deserve care. By keeping memory storage in the browser and using local inference, the application can reduce the need to transmit this personal information to a third-party AI provider. The intention is simple: your stories should remain yours. 2. The experience should not depend on a single AI provider. With an open-weight model and a transparent inference layer, developers can inspect the architecture, adapt the prompts, and explore compatible models. The project is not conceptually tied to a single hosted model or API. That flexibility matters for a tool whose purpose is to preserve stories over time. 3. AI should remain useful beyond a network connection. After the required resources have been downloaded and cached, a compatible local setup can support offline generation. No recurring hosted inference request is inherently necessary for each story. That makes the experience more independent of network availability and external service uptime, although it still depends on the user's hardware, browser, and locally available model files. 4. Open innovation makes experimentation accessible. I can experiment with different model sizes, adjust the writing instructions, and make the experience behave differently without redesigning the whole product around a closed API. There are real trade-offs: local models may be slower or less capable than larger hosted models, and the first download can be substantial. But for this particular application, privacy, control, and the possibility of continued use are valuable design goals. Open innovation is not simply about making software free. It is about giving people more control over the technology they depend on. The Spirit of It A favorite recipe. A familiar expression. A song that immediately brings someone to mind. A story told so many times that the family knows every word. Sometimes, what we fear losing isn't a grand story. It's one of these little details. That is the spirit behind The Last Light. The digital ofrenda draws inspiration from the remembrance traditions of Día de los Muertos, which honors the continuing connections people have with loved ones who have died. The intention is to approach that tradition with respect rather than reduce it to a Halloween effect. The AI writing studio adds a different dimension: it can help someone turn a scattered memory into something they can reread, share, edit, or preserve for the next generation. The result is still a human memory, shaped by the person who shared it. The AI is a writing companion, not a replacement for the person being remembered. And that distinction matters. Technology changes. Services disappear. Models evolve. But the stories people choose to preserve should not have to disappear with them. Some things disappear from the world. They don't have to disappear from our stories. That is The Last Light: a small experiment in making AI feel a little more personal, a little more private, and a little more human. 🕯️

articles.title: Apollo.io vs Lusha: Direct Phone & Email Enrichment Battle
articles.description: Apollo.io vs Lusha: Direct Phone & Email Enrichment Battle As Chief Operating Officer and Senior Systems Architect at HeliaTech Media, I evaluate B2B data infrastructure through a singular lens: data throughput, systemic friction, compliance surface area, and total cost of ownership (TCO). Modern sales and revenue operations (RevOps) stacks cannot afford the latency of disjointed tools. The choice between Apollo-Io and Lusha is not merely a preference for user interfaces; it is a fundamental architectural decision. You are choosing between a monolithic, end-to-end go-to-market (GTM) execution engine (Apollo) and a razor-sharp, lightweight enrichment and prospecting sniper rifle (Lusha). This masterclass provides a forensic teardown of both platforms, analyzing their databases, compliance engines, API capabilities, and economic models at scale. Executive Verdict: The 30-Second Summary Before diving into the architecture, here is the executive breakdown for engineering and RevOps leadership: Choose Apollo-Io if: You operate a high-volume outbound sales engine that requires native sequencing, CRM syncing, dialer integration, and massive prospecting volume under a single subscription. It is built for teams looking to consolidate their outbound stack. Choose Lusha if: Your organization prioritizes raw direct-dial accuracy over multichannel tooling, relies heavily on browser-based prospecting (LinkedIn/Sales Navigator), and requires strict, uncompromising compliance with global privacy frameworks (GDPR/CCPA) at the point of capture. Comprehensive Side-by-Side Comparison Matrix Evaluation Criteria Apollo-Io Lusha Core Architecture Monolithic GTM platform (Database + Sequencer + Dialer + Analytics) Specialized enrichment engine (Browser Extension + API + CRM Plugins) Database Scale 275M+ contacts, heavily weighted toward global SMB & Mid-Market 100M+ business profiles with rigorous real-time verification Direct Dial Accuracy Moderate to High (relies on continuous recrawling and decay algorithms) Very High (industry benchmark for direct-dial and mobile numbers) Pricing at Scale Tiered seat-based pricing with flexible credit consumption; highly cost-effective Strict credit-based metering; scales linearly, resulting in high enterprise costs Learning Curve Steep (requires configuration of filters, sequencing rules, and permissions) Minimal (intuitive browser extension and straightforward web app) API & Webhooks Robust REST API, bulk enrichment endpoints, and async webhooks Developer-friendly API, clear documentation, and standard CRM enrichment Ecosystem & Integrations Native Salesforce, HubSpot, Marketo, Zapier, and native email providers Deep integrations with Salesforce, HubSpot, Outreach, and Salesloft Security & Compliance SOC 2 Type II, GDPR/CCPA compliant frameworks SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, CCPA, and GDPR compliance with strict opt-out workflows Best For Full-cycle outbound teams, SDRs, and startups seeking stack consolidation Enterprise AEs, recruiters, and Account-Based Marketing (ABM) specialists Round 1: Architecture & Workflow Paradigms (Technical Teardown) Apollo-Io: The Monolithic GTM Operating System Apollo-Io approaches the market as an all-in-one infrastructure layer. Rather than acting strictly as an enrichment utility, Apollo integrates four core systems into a single relational database schema: The Data Lake: Hundreds of millions of contacts and companies mapped with technographic, firmographic, and intent signals. The Execution Engine: Built-in email sequencing, multi-step triggers, and dialer capabilities. The Analytics Layer: Attribution tracking, rep performance metrics, and email deliverability monitors (warm-up and domain health). The Enrichment Engine: Real-time API calls that append missing fields to CRM objects. The Architectural Trade-off: By housing data and execution in one platform, Apollo eliminates the data-loss latency typical of Zapier-bridged stacks. However, its expansive feature set can lead to interface bloat and steeper onboarding curves for non-technical users. Lusha: The Precision Enrichment Utility Lusha takes the opposite approach. It is built as a modular, lightweight insertion point into your existing workflow. Its architecture revolves around three primary access vectors: The Context-Aware Browser Extension: Instantly scrapes and matches DOM elements on LinkedIn, Salesforce, or corporate websites to serve verified direct dials and emails on demand. The Bulk Enrichment API: Designed for asynchronous, high-volume batch processing to clean and update existing CRM records. The Prospecting Web App: A clean, filtered interface designed for quick list building rather than long-term sequence management. The Architectural Trade-off: Lusha refuses to build a bloated outbound suite. It does not try to replace your sales engagement platform (SEP) like Outreach or Salesloft. Instead, it ensures that the data feeding those platforms is pristine. The trade-off is higher platform fragmentation; you must maintain separate tools for sequencing and calling. Round 2: Total Cost of Ownership & Scaling Math To evaluate the true economic impact, let us run a financial model across three operational tiers: 5,000, 50,000, and 500,000 monthly data operations (searches, reveals, and enrichments). Scenario A: 5,000 Monthly Operations (Small Outbound Team / 5 Seats) Apollo-Io (Professional Tier): Cost per seat: ~$79/month × 5 seats = $395/month Credits included: Generous export and mobile reveal limits (typically 1,200 mobile credits/seat/month). Total TCO: $4,740 / year (Includes sequencing and dialer). Lusha (Scale Tier): Cost per user + credit add-ons to hit 5,000 credits: ~$150/month × 5 seats = $750/month Total TCO: $9,000 / year (Requires a separate SEP subscription like Outreach at ~$100/seat/mo = $6,000/yr). Combined TCO: $15,000 / year. Scenario B: 50,000 Monthly Operations (Mid-Market RevOps / 25 Seats) Apollo-Io: Custom Organization Tier: ~$119/seat/month × 25 seats = $2,975/month Credits scale efficiently with organizational pooling. Total TCO: $35,700 / year (All-inclusive stack). Lusha: Enterprise Custom Tier with bulk API add-ons for 50,000 credits/month: ~$4,500/month Total TCO: $54,000 / year (Excluding external SEP costs). Scenario C: 500,000 Monthly Operations (Enterprise Scale / API Heavy) Apollo-Io API & Custom Enterprise: Enterprise data contracts running heavy API extraction: ~$8,000 – $12,000/month Total TCO: $96,000 – $144,000 / year. Lusha Enterprise API: High-volume enterprise enrichment contracts scale steeply due to proprietary verification costs: ~$18,000 – $25,000/month Total TCO: $216,000 – $300,000 / year. Mathematical Takeaway: Lusha commands a significant price premium per verified data point. For high-volume operations, Apollo-Io provides superior financial leverage. Lusha’s pricing model only pencils out if the higher accuracy of its phone numbers directly yields enough closed-won revenue to offset the data cost delta. Round 3: Integration Depth & Developer Ergonomics API & Webhook Performance Apollo-Io API Architecture: RESTful endpoints with JSON payloads. Rate Limits: Tiered dynamically based on enterprise contract levels. Standard tiers cap at 60 requests/minute; enterprise contracts scale significantly higher. Endpoints: Comprehensive access to contact search, organization search, email/phone enrichment, and job change tracking. Developer Experience: Good documentation, though asynchronous bulk processing can occasionally require custom retry logic to handle rate limit headers gracefully. Lusha API Architecture: Clean, purpose-built REST API focusing specifically on contact and company enrichment. Rate Limits: Transparent credit consumption headers returned with every API response (X-Credits-Left). Endpoints: Person Enrichment (by LinkedIn URL, email, or name/domain) and Company Enrichment. Developer Experience: Exceptional. Lusha’s API is lean, returning structured JSON with high fidelity. Integration into internal custom-built CRM tools or data lakes takes hours rather than days. Round 4: Critical Bottlenecks & Where Each Platform Fails No platform is without operational friction. As a systems architect, I stress-test tools to find their breaking points. Where Apollo-Io Fails Data Decay in Niche Verticals: While Apollo boasts a massive database, its broad coverage means niche industries (e.g., specialized biotech, regional supply chain logistics) suffer from higher email bounce rates and outdated phone numbers. UI Latency & Complexity: Because Apollo attempts to do everything, heavy filtering on large saved searches can cause UI lag. Permissions management across large enterprise teams can also become convoluted. Deliverability Risks: Because users can execute high-volume cold email campaigns directly out of Apollo using shared infrastructure, improper domain configuration can land your sending domains in spam traps if you do not strictly enforce custom SMTP/IMAP and dedicated IP setups. Where Lusha Fails Feature Churn & Monoculture: Lusha is fundamentally an enrichment tool. If you need advanced multi-touch sequencing, native cold-calling dialers, or intent-based trigger workflows, Lusha forces you to integrate third-party tools, increasing your stack's complexity and cost. Strict Credit Enforcement: Lusha’s credit system is unforgiving. If a user triggers an enrichment by accident on a profile, the credit is consumed. There are fewer safety nets for accidental bulk reveals compared to Apollo's pooled limits. Limited Firmographic Depth: While its contact data is pristine, Lusha’s technographic and deep firmographic intelligence trail behind dedicated market intelligence platforms. Concrete Real-World Decision Framework To make the final determination for your organization, apply this decision matrix based on your operational constraints. [Start Decision Tree] │ ├─► Do you require an all-in-one platform (Sequencer + Dialer + Database)? │ ├── YES ──► [CHOOSE APOLLO-IO] (/go/apollo-io) │ └── NO ──► Continue... ├─► Is direct-dial accuracy your #1 revenue metric (e.g., Enterprise Account Executives)? │ ├── YES ──► [CHOOSE LUSHA] (/go/lusha) ├─► What is your budget sensitivity at scale (>50k monthly operations)? │ ├── High Volume / Cost Sensitive ──► [CHOOSE APOLLO-IO] (/go/apollo-io) │ └── High Margin / Precision Focused ──► [CHOOSE LUSHA] (/go/lusha) ``` ### When to Strictly Choose Apollo-Io * You are a seed-to-Series B startup looking to consolidate 3–4 disparate sales tools (data provider, sequencer, dialer, CRM enricher) into a single bill. * Your outbound motion relies on high-volume email prospecting backed by automated workflows and trigger-based cadences. * You need broad geographical coverage across global SMB and mid-market accounts without breaking your RevOps budget. ### When to Strictly Choose Lusha * You run an enterprise outbound motion where every minute spent on a dead phone number destroys rep morale and productivity. * Your team lives inside LinkedIn Sales Navigator and requires instant, zero-friction inline data revelation via browser extension. * You operate in strict regulatory environments where data provenance, immediate opt-out compliance (CCPA/GDPR), and transparent data sourcing are mandatory for legal sign-off. --- ## Official Evaluation & Deployment CTAs To test these architectures within your own stack, use the official deployment portals below: * **Deploy Apollo-Io:** Audit the database, test the sequencing engine, and model your team's TCO via the official [Apollo-Io Platform Portal](/go/apollo-io). * **Deploy Lusha:** Test direct-dial match rates, install the browser extension, and evaluate API endpoints via the official [Lusha Enterprise Portal](/go/lusha). *** *Architectural Analysis Complete. Select your deployment path based on data volume, workflow consolidation needs, and economic constraints.* *Originally benchmarked and published on [HeliaTech Media](https://heliatech.online/blog/apollo-io-vs-lusha) — Independent SaaS & Cloud Architecture Intelligence.*

articles.title: How to Check If a Whisper Model Is Available Before Calling a Transcription API
articles.description: Short answer: Check GET /v1/ai/models first, cache the selected model's available value for about 60 seconds, and call POST /v1/audio/transcriptions only when it is true; the current ASR catalog returns available: false, so show “transcription temporarily unavailable” for the invoice instead. For a gaming company turning supplier invoice audio into structured fields, make model readiness a hard gate. The provider behind it can change without forcing the rest of the pipeline to change, provided the replacement exposes an equivalent readiness decision. The useful contract is small: ready, unavailable, or status-check failure. Keep that contract inside the worker and the invoice state machine. What is the invoice bill actually made of? Audio duration is the dominant input to the transcription bill. The model catalog lists qwen3-asr-flash at $0.01176 per minute; a 30-minute batch therefore represents 30 billable minutes, or $0.3528 at that listed rate. That arithmetic is not the design decision. The design decision is to avoid submitting the same media while the service is known to be unavailable, because repeated attempts add control-plane noise without making the recording shorter. Retention has a different cost. I would keep the supplier's original audio for the business-defined dispute or reprocessing window, then retain the extracted invoice fields and a compact audit record rather than an unbounded media archive. The trade is explicit: deleting the source reduces retention exposure, but it removes the ability to replay a disputed transcription. A failed readiness check must never be “fixed” by keeping or uploading more copies of the same audio. The invoice record should therefore carry a retryable status and the reason for the gate. It should not carry an empty set of fields that looks like a successful extraction. The gate is binary. That distinction becomes important when a supplier sends the same recording again after a failed attempt. The worker should identify the invoice and its audio object before making the status decision, record that the attempt was rejected because the selected ASR model was unavailable, and leave the item eligible for a later retry. It should not create a partial field record, mark the invoice as processed, or infer that an empty transcript means the supplier omitted data. A later health check can reopen the retry path after the model reports available: true, but it cannot recover information that the pipeline discarded under a success-shaped result. How can I check whether a Whisper model is available before calling transcription? Use the collection endpoint when the model identifier is configured by deployment. Its response contains an available boolean for each model. Treat that value as a short-lived admission signal, not as a guarantee that a later request cannot fail. import json import os import urllib.error import urllib.request BASE_URL = os.environ["API_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/") MODEL_ID = os.environ["ASR_MODEL_ID"] def get_json(path): request = urllib.request. Request( BASE_URL + path, headers={"Authorization": "Bearer " + os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]}, method="GET", ) try: with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=10) as response: if response.status < 200 or response.status >= 300: raise RuntimeError( "model status check failed: HTTP " + str(response.status) return json.load(response) except urllib.error.HTTPError as error: body = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace") "model status check failed: HTTP " + str(error.code) + " " + body def model_is_ready(): models = get_json("/ai/models") for model in models.get("data", []): if model.get("id") == MODEL_ID: return model.get("available") is True return False if not model_is_ready(): raise RuntimeError("transcription temporarily unavailable") print("ASR model is ready; the worker may submit the transcription request") The example stops at the gate because the supplied contract does not define the multipart fields for the transcription request. That is deliberate. A runnable example that invents an audio field would teach a false contract. The production caller still needs to check the transcription response status, expose the actual error body, and treat a later failure as a race with readiness rather than silently losing the invoice. If the status check receives HTTP 429, use bounded exponential backoff and honor Retry-After; a tight loop turns a service limit into more pressure. The same rule applies to the periodic checker. For a submission retry, use a client-supplied idempotency key where the write contract supports one, so a network timeout does not create a second processing record. Which readiness contract fits supplier invoices? The comparison should be about the failure boundary, not a brand ranking. Option Useful distinction Boundary for this workflow OpenAI Whisper API A direct transcription API with a model and uploaded audio request The application still owns readiness, retry, and retention policy Google Cloud Speech-to-Text Google documents synchronous and asynchronous recognition paths The team must choose the lifecycle and region behavior that matches invoice volume Amazon Transcribe AWS documents job-oriented transcription for longer-running processing A job state is not the same as an immediately available model A REST gateway with a model catalog A machine-readable status can be checked before media submission The worker must respect available: false and deal with stale cache data For this workflow, the fourth option is valuable only if its status is explicit and the worker uses it as a gate. Infrai's relevant advantages are that the backend is exposed through one plain REST API and that one key spans 295 routes across 20 modules, so the invoice service can keep its internal contract while the service behind that capability changes. Any language or runtime that can send HTTP can use that surface; no SDK-specific transcription integration is required. That simplifies the boundary, but it does not make an unavailable ASR model available. Anthropic and Gemini are sensible alternatives for the later structured extraction step when the team wants a model-specific JSON workflow, while OpenAI's direct transcription path is a better comparison for this media boundary. Each choice still requires its own availability, retention, and error policy; a capable extraction model cannot compensate for an unavailable transcription service. The limitation matters today: the ASR catalog reports available: false. If an invoice must be transcribed immediately, use a provider whose documented transcription service is ready and accept the provider-specific integration. If the broader system values one REST contract across several backend capabilities, evaluate the gateway again after ASR readiness returns. Those are different decisions. The same caution applies to adjacent capabilities. Real-time voice sessions have pending key status and are limited to the western region, and there is no dedicated moderation endpoint; text or image moderation requires a chat model with a JSON schema fallback. Neither fact should be smuggled into an invoice transcription promise. How should caching and recovery work? Cache the status for roughly 60 seconds, with both the model id and the observation time in the key. That interval avoids hammering the models endpoint while keeping an outage visible within a bounded period. Never turn a status-check error into ready, and never let a stale true bypass the response-status check on the transcription request. Run a periodic health check separately from invoice traffic. When the model flips back to available: true, the checker can mark workers eligible again; it should not manufacture an invoice result for files rejected during the outage. Those files need an explicit retry state. A standard queue is at-least-once, so the consumer must make its state transition idempotent. The user-facing path should be plain: return “transcription temporarily unavailable,” preserve the invoice's retryable state, and retain the original upload according to policy. A generic timeout or an empty field set is harder to operate because neither tells the reviewer whether the supplier's document was bad or the transcription service was unavailable. articles.title: I Had 5,000 Screenshots and Couldn’t Find Any, So I Built: SnapRecall-Type What You Remember, Find the Screenshot
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady What I Built SnapRecall is a screenshot search tool. It watches your screenshots folder, lets an AI model read every image in the background, and builds a private search index. Later, you type whatever you remember about the screenshot ("rahul payment 2500", "docker permission error", "wo flight ticket wala") and the matching screenshots show up. How I got the idea I take a lot of screenshots. A payment confirmation, a WhatsApp chat I might need as proof, an error message I want to Google later, a ticket, a recipe, a random detail from a group chat. I never organize them, because the whole point of a screenshot is that it takes one second. The cost shows up later. My screenshots folder has thousands of files, all named like this: screenshot_2026-10-24-14-55-16.png screenshot_2026-10-24-14-55-41.png screenshot_2026-10-24-15-02-07.png When I need one specific image, those names tell me nothing. I end up scrolling through hundreds of nearly identical thumbnails, squinting at each one, and sometimes giving up. It is not a big problem, but it happens often, and it is exactly the kind of tedious work that a computer should do instead of me. When I read the "slow and steady" theme, this was the first thing I thought of. It is a task that should happen quietly in the background, with no effort from me, while I do something else. Two ideas, one choice I had two possible solutions: Rename on save. The moment a screenshot is taken, an AI reads it, summarizes it, and renames the file with the important words. A WhatsApp chat about rent becomes something like whatsapp_rahul_rent_payment.png. Search by memory. Leave the files alone. When I cannot find a screenshot, I type the words I remember from inside it, and the app shows me the matches. Renaming looked simple, but when I thought it through, it had problems. A filename is one guess about what I will remember later, and the AI's guess is often not the thing I remember. A screenshot of a chat could be filed under the contact's name, the topic, or the amount, and I might search by any of them. Renaming files can also break references in other apps or sync tools, and after a few thousand files, long auto-generated names start to look the same again. Search works with whatever I happen to remember, and it does not touch my files. So I chose search as the core, and I treat smart renaming as a possible add-on for later (with a preview and an undo, not silent changes). Who it is for Anyone with a messy screenshots folder: students who screenshot notes, developers who save error messages, and people who screenshot payments, chats and tickets as proof. I also built it with Hindi and Hinglish in mind, because that is how I actually think and type. A lot of the text in my screenshots is in Hindi or mixed, and I did not want a tool that only works for clean English. Features Background indexing: new screenshots are picked up automatically soon after they are saved A slow, throttled backfill of your old screenshots, so a big backlog never needs your attention A vision model reads each screenshot and produces a short summary, tags, an app type (chat, payment, code, error, ticket...) and the text it can see Hybrid search: keyword matching for exact names, amounts and error codes, plus semantic search for vague memories English, Hindi and Hinglish queries A simple React interface with a thumbnail grid, a larger preview, and live indexing progress with pause and resume Demo Code GitHub repo How I Built It The stack Backend: Python and FastAPI Frontend: React (Vite, TypeScript) Storage: SQLite for everything, with FTS5 for keyword search and sqlite-vec for vectors Folder watching: watchdog Models: Gemma for reading screenshots, plus an embedding model for semantic search I chose SQLite on purpose. For a personal tool, one file with no server to run is a big advantage, and it keeps the whole thing light on a laptop. The pipeline Screenshots folder | v Watcher + folder scanner -> job queue (SQLite) one image at a time, with a pause downscale image -> Gemma: summary, tags, app type, visible text embed the combined text SQLite: metadata + keyword index + vector index ^ React UI -> FastAPI -> hybrid search (keyword + semantic, merged) For each screenshot, the worker downscales the image (so it does not send more pixels than needed), asks Gemma for a short summary, a few tags, the type of screenshot, and the important text it can read, then turns that combined text into an embedding. Everything is stored in SQLite next to the original file path. Why the search is hybrid I tried to think about how I actually look for screenshots, and I realized there are two very different cases. Sometimes I remember something exact: a name, an amount like "2500", an error code. Keyword search is best for this, because semantic search can blur exact tokens together. Other times my memory is vague: "that screenshot of the bus ticket" or "the chat where we decided the date". Here, keyword search fails if the exact words do not match, but semantic search can still find it because it matches meaning. So SnapRecall runs both searches and merges the two ranked lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, which rewards results that rank well in either list without needing to compare their scores directly. It is a simple technique, and it covers both ways I search. Slow and steady, on purpose This is where the theme became a design rule instead of a slogan. Reading thousands of images with a model is heavy work. If a tool tries to do it all at once, it either freezes your computer or burns through your API limits and fails halfway. So the indexer is built to be patient: It processes one image at a time, with a configurable pause between images It backs off and retries when the API rate-limits it, instead of treating that as a failure It can pause itself when a daily request budget is reached, and it can be paused and resumed from the interface If the app is closed or crashes, it picks up where it stopped when it starts again You can keep working while it runs. It is the opposite of a tool that demands your attention. Local first, then hosted, and why I changed My original plan was fully local: Gemma through Ollama, Tesseract for OCR, everything on my own machine. Then I looked at my laptop. It is old and weak, and running a vision model on it would be painfully slow, if it ran at all. So for this submission I changed course and used Gemma 4 through the Gemini API. The backend does not become heavy this way: it only watches a folder, stores data in SQLite and serves a few endpoints, so my laptop handles it fine, and the heavy model work happens remotely. I also turned off the OCR step in hosted mode, because Gemma already returns the text it sees. I built the model layer behind a provider switch, so the same pipeline can point to a hosted API or to a local Ollama server. That was partly a practical decision and partly a way to keep the project honest about the open vs hosted tradeoff, which I explain below. One thing to be clear about: in hosted mode, the embeddings come from a hosted embedding model that is not open-source, so that part of the stack is not open. I also used an AI assistant to help plan the architecture and write parts of the code. I am still testing how well it all works together, which brings me to the status at the end of this post. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? The prompt asks some direct questions, so I will answer them directly, including the places where my answer is "not yet" or "not really". Does running your own model mean it works without internet? In principle, yes, and that is one of the main reasons I picked an open model family. In the mode I used for this submission, no: I ran Gemma through a hosted API, so it needs an internet connection. The project is designed so that a local Ollama setup should work offline once the models are downloaded, but I have not been able to test that on my own hardware, so I will not claim it works. Does it keep personal messages and files on your own machine? This is the point that matters most for this particular project. Screenshots are one of the most private things on a phone or laptop: OTPs, bank messages, personal chats, ID photos. Uploading thousands of them to a third party is a real cost, and many people would rightly refuse. In hosted mode, my screenshots do go to the model provider, so please do not treat that mode as private. What open weights give me is a private option. The same model family can run on a machine the user controls, and a user who cares about privacy can choose that path. With a closed vision API, there would be no such option: the only way to use it is to send the images out. Does it let you set it up once and never pay again? With a local model, that is the idea: after the setup, indexing 10,000 screenshots costs only electricity. With the hosted route I used, I am on a free tier with limits, and those limits shaped the design directly. The worker is throttled, it respects rate limits, and it has a daily request budget, because indexing a big backlog through a hosted API would otherwise hit those limits fast. A closed API charged per image would add a cost on every re-index, which matters a lot for a tool whose job is to process thousands of images. Where did the open approach work better than a closed one? The honest answer is flexibility, not raw quality. Because Gemma's weights are open, the same model was available to me as a hosted API when my laptop could not run it, and it is available to someone with a stronger machine to run privately. I could pick the deployment that matched my hardware, and I can change that choice later without rewriting the project. Prize Categories Best Use of Gemma: Gemma is the model that actually reads the screenshots. Its summary, tags, app type and visible text are what the whole search index is built from, so without it the project does not work. I used Gemma 4 through the Gemini API. Where This Stands This is an idea I took from a real annoyance to a working design in a short time, and it still needs testing. Thank you for taking the time to read this.

articles.title: Week 3's DEV challenge
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady Lazy Meal Diary: an offline cooking helper for students, on my phone My PC is still broken. Last week's post was about the day it died, and it's still not fixed, so this build also had to run on the only computer I have left: my Redmi 13. The problem Student cooking has the same loop every week. You cook something decent on Tuesday, forget it by Friday, and stand in front of the same few ingredients with no idea what to make. I wanted a diary I could talk to in one line, one that remembers what I cooked and suggests something similar later. What I built App: PocketPal AI (open-source), running fully on the phone Model: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (q4_k_m, about 1.1 GB), an open-weight model A system prompt that makes it a meal diary for a Nigerian student with one burner and a small budget One dedicated chat for the whole week How the "memory" works The model has no memory of its own. PocketPal keeps the chat, and the model re-reads the whole chat every time I send a message. So as long as I keep one chat open, Tuesday's meal is still in front of it on Friday. Why open matters here It works offline, so no data is spent. My eating habits and budget stay on my phone and not on someone else's server. It costs nothing per message, so I never pay for it. I can change the model, the prompt, and the generation settings. What worked I logged "Tuesday: egg and indomie with tomato" and "Wednesday: beans and garri". On Friday I asked for something similar to Tuesday's meal, and the model correctly named "egg and indomie with tomato". Replies came in about 2 seconds after the model loaded, at around 6 tokens per second. What didn't A repetition loop. My first attempt made the model write a random recipe and then repeat "1/4 cup chopped cilantro" over and over. I fixed it by lowering temperature, raising the repeat penalty, and capping the reply length. It ignored my "one short line" rule. When I logged a meal, it often answered with a recipe instead of a short confirmation. It ignored my new ingredients. On Friday I said I had eggs, rice, and pepper. It recalled Tuesday's meal but used none of those ingredients, and it invented "egg noodles". A 1.5B model on a phone can recall what's in the chat, but it doesn't follow detailed instructions well. Honest note This is a prompt-driven tool, not a trained model, and a long chat could overload a small model's context. I tested four messages in one chat and not with another student. Next I'd try a 3B model, store meals in a small file so memory doesn't depend on chat length, and test it with a real classmate. Once my PC is fixed, I'd like to turn this into a proper build with a bigger model and a saved meal log, so the memory doesn't depend on a chat staying short. Screenshots (Attach: the cilantro loop, the Tuesday entry reply, and the Friday reply.)

articles.title: LazyMorning — Your Overnight Life Assistant
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady What I Built Mornings are often ruined by a barrage of questions: What was I working on yesterday? Which deadlines are due today? What do I need to tackle first? This morning decision fatigue drains our best mental energy before the day even begins. LazyMorning is an overnight personal life assistant designed to let you wake up with complete clarity and zero panic. While you sleep, LazyMorning analyzes your active tasks, captured notes, upcoming deadlines, and approved documents to prepare a serene, focused Morning Briefing delivered right as you start your day. What it does: Today's Focus: Synthesizes a calming, single-sentence priority focus for the morning. Top 3 Priorities: Extracts the three highest-impact tasks with explicit reasoning and urgency tags. Upcoming Deadlines: Clear timeline of impending deliverables so nothing slips through the cracks. Unfinished Items: Quick tally of pending items requiring future attention. Suggested First Step: Gives you an immediate, low-friction, concrete first action (e.g. "Spend 10 minutes reviewing the first slide") to kick off your day with calm momentum instead of paralysis. Who gets to be a little lazier because of it? Developers, students, founders, and busy professionals who want to reclaim peaceful mornings. Instead of spending 30 minutes every morning triaging sticky notes, Slack messages, and todo lists, you open your LazyMorning dashboard, sip your coffee with our relaxed sloth mascot, and know exactly what to do next. Demo 🌐 Live Deployed App: https://lazymorning.onrender.com/ 📖 Interactive API Documentation (Swagger): https://lazymorning.onrender.com/docs Code Check out the full open-source repository on GitHub: 👉 https://github.com/abhinavnayak21/LazyMorning-x-MLH abhinavnayak21 / LazyMorning-x-MLH 🦥 LazyMorning — Your Overnight Life Assistant "Slow plans, brighter days." Built for the "Slow and Steady" Open-Source AI Challenge. LazyMorning is a privacy-first, 100% local personal morning assistant. While you sleep, LazyMorning reviews your active tasks, notes, deadlines, and approved files to prepare a serene, focused morning briefing—eliminating morning decision fatigue and friction. 📸 Design & Experience Crafted to match modern, calming aesthetics with an adorable mascot and clean cards: Dashboard: Daily greeting, Today's Focus hero banner, 4 vital metrics (Top Priorities, Upcoming Deadlines, Pending Tasks, Total Notes), latest briefing summary, and quick actions. Morning Briefing: Today's Focus, Top 3 Priorities (with reasoning and deadlines), Upcoming Deadlines list, Unfinished Items, and a gentle Suggested First Step. Notes: Create, organize, tag, and search thoughts and ideas. Tasks: Track priorities (High, Medium, Low), due dates, and instant checkbox completion. Imported Files: Scan and import local .txt… View on GitHub How I Built It LazyMorning is designed from the ground up around open-source AI and private local-first computing: 1. Open-Source AI Architecture Model: Qwen 2.5 (7B Instruct) — a state-of-the-art open-weight model renowned for structured reasoning, nuance, and concise summarization. Hybrid Inference Pipeline: Local Ollama: Runs 100% locally on personal machines via Ollama (qwen2.5:7b). Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared): Allows remote deployment on Render to securely reach local Ollama instances over an encrypted Cloudflare Tunnel without public port forwarding. Cloudflare Workers AI: Cloudflare’s serverless GPU edge option running @cf/qwen/qwen2.5-7b-instruct for 24/7 cloud availability. Zero-Crash Local Fallback Engine: If Ollama or the network is ever unreachable, an intelligent rule-based synthesizer steps in automatically, ensuring you never miss a briefing. Hallucination Validator: AI outputs are strictly cross-referenced against the SQLite database to ensure the model never invents ghost tasks or fake deadlines. 2. Tech Stack Frontend: Streamlit styled with custom modern CSS and base64 vector art to create a warm, calming aesthetic with our sloth mascot. Backend: FastAPI with async REST routing and OpenAPI documentation. Database: SQLite with SQLAlchemy ORM for lightweight, durable local persistence. Overnight Scheduler: APScheduler running in-process for automated morning digest generation at configurable local wake-up times. Automated Tests: Comprehensive Pytest suite covering CRUD operations, file security gates, AI fallback, and hallucination filters (100% pass rate). 3. Privacy & File Approval Gate To prevent accidental data leakage, imported local .txt and .md files enter a pending state. Only files explicitly toggled to "✅ Approved for AI" are included in the morning briefing context. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Your daily notes, personal reflections, project roadmaps, and client meeting takeaways are sensitive personal data. Sending them to closed, proprietary cloud AI APIs: Risks privacy: Exposes private thoughts and proprietary work to third-party data collection and training pipelines. Introduces toll booths: Closed APIs charge per-token fees, making automated overnight background cron jobs expensive over time. Creates fragility: Closed services suffer outages, policy changes, and sudden price hikes. Open innovation changes the game. By using open-weight models like Qwen 2.5 running locally via Ollama or over self-controlled Cloudflare tunnels, LazyMorning demonstrates that users don't need to sacrifice their privacy or pay monthly API subscriptions to get intelligent, automated life assistance. My Agent Session Built with pair-programming assistance from Antigravity. You can view or replay the session here: The Lazy Payoff Saved 20–30 minutes every morning: Eliminates the cognitive load of opening 5 different tools (Notes app, Todoist, Markdown files, Slack reminders) just to figure out what to do first. Zero Morning Panic: Instead of waking up to an overwhelming wall of 20 unorganized tasks, you get Top 3 Priorities and a gentle Suggested First Step. Effortless Overnight Automation: The in-process APScheduler generates everything before you open your eyes. You literally wake up to finished organization. Prize Categories Slow and Steady Grand Prize Best Use of Open-Weight Models (Qwen 2.5 & Ollama) Best Local-First / Privacy-Preserving AI Application Most Creative / Fun UI & Mascot Design

articles.title: AI Cleanup: How Freelancers Can Earn Without Writing Code
articles.description: Freelancers often feel stuck between wanting more projects and fearing they need to learn programming first. The good news is there are jobs that only require a basic understanding of AI and the ability to run a few tools. This post explains what AI cleanup is, where to find gigs, which skills you need, real-world pricing, and a step-by-step plan to start earning. What Is AI Cleanup? AI cleanup means using artificial-intelligence models to remove noise, duplicates, or labeling errors from data, images, or text. Typical tasks include: Removing unwanted backgrounds from photos. Auto-correcting spelling in user comments. Sorting a mislabeled image dataset. According to Kompas.com, AI cleanup services are in high demand as companies look to speed up their data pipelines. Platforms That List AI Cleanup Projects Upwork – Search under Data Cleaning or Image Annotation. Many clients include the phrase “AI cleanup” in the job description. Fiverr – Create a gig titled something like “Clean your image dataset with AI.” Gigs start at $5 (≈ Rp 75 000) and can be upsold with premium packages. Sribulancer – An Indonesian platform that often posts local-language projects, e.g., “Bersihkan dataset komentar forum.” Freelance.com – Offers short-term projects with clear daily budgets. All of these platforms use escrow to protect payments, which reduces the risk of non-payment. Skills You Need Skill Difficulty How to Learn Basic AI concepts (supervised vs unsupervised) Low Free courses on Coursera or YouTube – search “AI basics for non-programmers.” Using the Cleanformer tool Medium Official docs: https://cleanformer.ai/docs OpenAI API (ChatGPT, DALL·E) for text-to-text cleaning OpenAI’s tutorial pages; a one-line Python example is enough. Result evaluation (accuracy checks, visual inspection) Practice with sample datasets on Kaggle, e.g., Cats vs Dogs You don’t need to write complex code. Many tools provide drag-and-drop interfaces or simple command-line commands. Real-World Project Examples and Pricing 1. Clean an E-Commerce Image Dataset Description: 2,000 product photos with inconsistent backgrounds, some blurry, and many duplicates. Tool: Cleanformer + a tiny Python script for duplicate detection. Time: 12-15 hours. Rate: Rp 800 000 – Rp 1 000 000 (depends on speed). 2. Remove Spam from Blog Comments Description: 5,000 comments, 12 % are spam or ads. Tool: OpenAI Moderation API. Time: 6-8 hours. Rate: Rp 300 000 – Rp 500 000. 3. Fix Typos in Legal Documents Description: 50 PDF files (≈150 pages) with spelling errors and inconsistent formatting. Tool: GPT-4 with a custom prompt for language correction. Time: 10-12 hours. Rate: Rp 400 000 – Rp 600 000. These rates come from several Upwork listings posted over the past three months. Prices can vary based on project complexity and freelancer reputation. Practical Steps to Start an AI Cleanup Project Create a Focused Profile – Add AI Cleanup Specialist to your headline and showcase before-after samples in your portfolio. Pick One Tool to Master – Start with Cleanformer before expanding to other utilities. Take Small Jobs First – Target budgets of Rp 200 000 – Rp 400 000 to build a rating. Use a Proposal Template – Outline the workflow, time estimate, and sample output. Ask for Feedback – Positive reviews boost your chances of higher-paying gigs. Below is a short proposal you can copy-paste: **Subject:** Proposal AI Cleanup for Your Image Dataset Hi [Client Name], I can clean your 2,000 product images by: 1. Removing background noise with Cleanformer. 2. Detecting and deleting duplicate files. 3. Delivering a zip folder with renamed, uniform images. Estimated time: 14 hours. Cost: Rp 850 000 (including revisions). Let me know if you have any questions! Best, [Your Name] Risks and How to Mitigate Them Data Quality: Very noisy datasets may still need manual spot-checks. Always include a quality-check step. API Costs: OpenAI API charges per token. Estimate the cost before quoting a price. Competition: Many freelancers offer similar services. Differentiate yourself with speed, visual quality, or an extra statistical report. Summary AI cleanup = AI-powered data, image, or text cleaning; demand is growing. Main platforms: Upwork, Fiverr, Sribulancer, Freelance.com. Key skills: basic AI theory, Cleanformer, OpenAI API, result evaluation. Typical rates: Rp 200 000 – Rp 1 000 000 per project, depending on volume and complexity. Getting started: craft a niche profile, take small gigs, use a proposal template, and collect reviews. If you want to boost your income without learning to code, AI cleanup is a realistic first step. Follow for daily AI, career, and money-making insights!

articles.title: Is It Drift or Is It the Game? How to Tell Before You Open Your Controller
articles.description: Your character walks left on its own. Your camera slowly pans up. Before you reach for a screwdriver, stop: many of these symptoms are not stick drift at all. A game setting, a deadzone problem, or a second input device can look exactly like a broken stick. Checking in the right order saves you from opening a controller that was never faulty. Start outside the game Drift means the controller itself is sending movement when you are not touching the stick. So test the controller, not the game. Connect it to a PC, open a browser-based tester, and leave both sticks untouched for 30 seconds. You can test your controller online in a couple of minutes, with no download. Watch the stick dot and the axis values. If the dot stays centered and the values stay at zero, the hardware is probably fine. If the dot creeps in one direction, or an axis value sits above zero at rest, you have real drift to investigate. This one step changes the whole repair plan. A centered stick points to software. A creeping stick points to cleaning, recalibration, or a worn sensor. Signs it is probably the game Try these clues before you blame the hardware: The problem happens in only one game, but the same controller is steady in other games and in the tester. Camera movement changes when you change in-game sensitivity, invert settings, or aim assist. The issue stops when you unplug a second controller, a flight stick, or another input device. A game update, a new controller profile, or a Steam Input layout changed the behavior. In these cases, reset the in-game controls to default, check the deadzone setting, and try a different controller profile. On PC, also check whether Steam Input is remapping your sticks in a way the game does not expect. Signs it is probably drift Drift is more likely when: The tester shows movement with your hands off the controller. The same direction creeps in every game and in menus. The stick does not return cleanly to center after you release it. Increasing the deadzone hides the problem, but only for a while, and you need a larger deadzone each week. A deadzone increase is a useful test, not a cure. If a small deadzone hides the movement, the sensor may still be borderline. If you need a very large deadzone to stop the creep, the sensor is likely worn. A simple test order that works Test at rest in a browser tester and note which stick and direction moves. Test in a second game. If only one game is affected, check that game's settings first. Clean around the stick base with compressed air, rotate the stick slowly in full circles, and retest. Recalibrate or reset the controller, check for a firmware update, and retest. Only then decide about repair: a module replacement for a worn sensor, or a repair shop if soldering is involved. When opening the controller makes sense Open it only after the tester confirms drift and after cleaning and recalibration have failed. At that point you are fixing a known sensor problem, not guessing. Keep track of screws, take a photo before you disconnect anything, and do not force a module that does not match your model. If the tester is steady and the problem follows one game, keep the screwdriver in the drawer. Fix the setting, the profile, or the conflicting input device instead. That is the fastest repair of all, because there was nothing to repair in the hardware.

articles.title: Weekend - China warns of countermeasures as US Treasury widens tech investment curbs to biotech
articles.description: The proposal adds to already tense US-China relations and keeps headline risk elevated for Chinese technology and biotech stocks, including US-listed ADRs and the Hang Seng Tech index. Biotech is the sector most directly exposed, since it is the newly targeted industry and has relied more heavily on cross-border funding than areas already under restriction. Beijing has not named the countermeasures it might take, and that vagueness tends to keep investors cautious until the response becomes clear. A long public comment period leaves time for negotiation, but it also stretches the uncertainty out for months, which could weigh on risk appetite toward China-exposed assets and the offshore yuan if rhetoric escalates. -- Washington wants to stop US capital from funding China’s next generation of strategic technology, and Beijing is signalling that it will not take the move quietly. Summary: On Thursday the US Treasury proposed a rule expanding the Outbound Investment Security Program, tightening limits on US investment in hypersonics, quantum, high-performance computing, supercomputing and AI in China, Russia and North Korea The rule also adds biotechnology to the targeted sectors, an addition sought by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent China’s commerce ministry said on Saturday the move discriminatorily widens China-related restrictions, overstretches national security and would damage bilateral economic ties Beijing said it will monitor developments and reserves the right to take unspecified countermeasures The proposal faces a public comment period before a final rule is issued Separately, the State Department this week sanctioned five Chinese companies linked to former Google engineer Linwei Ding, convicted this year of stealing AI trade secrets, drawing further objections from Beijing China has urged the United States to reconsider a proposed rule that would further restrict American investment in its technology sector, warning that the measure would harm trade relations and that Beijing reserves the right to retaliate. China’s commerce ministry voiced firm opposition on Saturday in a statement carried by the state-run Global Times, according to a report by The Hill. A ministry spokesperson said the proposal widens China-related investment restrictions in a discriminatory way and described it as a classic example of stretching the concept of national security too far. The ministry said it would watch subsequent developments closely, warned the rule would damage economic ties between the two countries, and said China retains the right to take corresponding measures, without specifying what those might be. The US Treasury Department unveiled the proposal on Thursday. It would expand existing restrictions under the Outbound Investment Security Program covering hypersonic systems, quantum information technologies, high-performance computing, supercomputing and artificial intelligence. The program aims to stop a small group of countries designated as foreign adversaries, namely China, Russia and North Korea, from using US capital to advance their own technological capabilities. The proposed rule would also bring the biotechnology industry within the program’s scope, an addition that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had pushed for, according to a department press release. Bessent said the changes would strengthen the program and prevent adversaries from using American investment to build critical technologies that threaten US national security. The measure must go through a public comment period before Treasury issues a final version, leaving room for revisions and for further diplomatic exchanges in the meantime. The proposal lands days after the State Department imposed sanctions on five Chinese companies connected to Linwei Ding, a former Google engineer convicted earlier this year of stealing trade secrets related to artificial intelligence. Beijing also objected to those penalties, saying they seriously harm the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese businesses. Taken together, the two moves underline Washington’s widening focus on technology and capital flows as a front in its rivalry with China. Beijing’s eventual response is now the key variable for investors and policymakers alike. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
